title: Week of 17–21 August 2026 · Days 160–164
in_one_line: The commission spent the week on two witnesses who would not or could not give it a straight account — Vusimuzi Matlala, who declined most questions on self-incrimination grounds, and Fadiel Adams, who spent three days revising his own evidence — while a documentary session laid out message traffic about surveillance equipment.

what_happened.heading: Matlala appears, and mostly declines
what_happened.body: Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala took the stand after several postponements, following a fire alarm evacuation that delayed the start. He repeatedly declined to answer questions about the disputed R228-million SAPS health services contract awarded to Medicare24 and about alleged payments to police officials, relying on his right against self-incrimination because of a pending criminal matter in the Specialised Commercial Crimes Court. He did answer on some points: he denied knowing then Police Minister Senzo Mchunu, denied any relationship with Major-General Feroz Khan, and gave evidence about his dealings with Brown Mogotsi, acknowledging that Mogotsi had asked him for money. He also alleged that investigators had pressured him while he was in custody to implicate senior police officials. Justice Madlanga directed that a supplementary affidavit setting out the legal basis for the refusals be filed, with a replying affidavit and heads of argument due by 18:00 on 22 August 2026, and set his evidence to resume on 24 and 25 August.
what_happened.tier_note: Tier 2 reporting (TimesLIVE, The Citizen, Cape Times, SABC News). No transcript consulted.

what_happened.heading: A documentary session on surveillance equipment
what_happened.body: No witness gave oral evidence. Evidence leader Advocate Matthew Chaskalson SC took the commission through communications extracted from devices belonging to the late taxi industry figure Msibi. The material was said to show negotiations to acquire surveillance and signal-jamming equipment, including IMSI-catcher or 'grabber' technology, and an alleged plan to market it to the government of Eswatini. Chaskalson told the commission that three men, including Katiso 'KT' Molefe and businessman Steve Motsumi, allegedly presented themselves as representatives of the South African state in dealings with foreign suppliers. Other material touched on tender-rigging and a cannabis project. The commission did not establish whether any transaction was completed — an important limit on what this evidence shows.
what_happened.tier_note: Tier 2 and Tier 3 reporting. Extraction reports and message exhibits not seen directly.

what_happened.heading: Adams finally gives evidence
what_happened.body: Fadiel Adams, leader of the National Coloured Congress and a Member of Parliament, began the substantive evidence that had been postponed from 11 August. He told the commission he had found an envelope marked 'Top Secret' pushed under his parliamentary office door in late October 2024, containing material about alleged irregular procurement and misuse of secret service funds. He disputed IDAC's account of a 6 January 2025 interview in Cape Town, saying a supplementary affidavit marked A1 attributed to IDAC investigator Dylan Perumal did not match the statements taken from him. He conceded he had been untruthful about when he learned of earlier correspondence, having blamed a malfunctioning laptop, and denied acting as a conduit for criminal cartels.

what_happened.heading: The dead-man problem
what_happened.body: Evidence leader Advocate Lee Segeels-Ncube pressed Adams on his reliance on the late General Andre Lincoln, who died in May 2025, as the source of his allegations, and on when he opened criminal cases in Cape Town and Johannesburg in October 2024. Adams said he had written to then Police Minister Senzo Mchunu within a day of opening the cases. Justice Madlanga questioned how Lincoln, described as being in Cape Town and incapacitated, could have intercepted dockets. The sitting was adjourned so that Adams could listen to recordings — described as roughly two hours — of his January 2025 meeting with IDAC officials before questioning resumed.
what_happened.tier_note: Tier 2 reporting (The Citizen, SABC News). Exact date of the adjournment direction is inferred.

what_happened.heading: Retractions, and an altered document claim
what_happened.body: Adams retracted his earlier account of contacting a man he knows as 'Elvis' from Orlando Police Station, saying instead that he met Elvis at a tyre shop and that the two arrived at the station together. He gave evidence about a fifth affidavit taken from him by IDAC investigator Dylan Perumal on the evening of 6 January 2025 — an affidavit bearing an official IDAC stamp, unlike four earlier statements taken the same day — and said Perumal came to his home at night while on a call with then IDAC head Advocate Andrea Johnson. Adams alleged that his section 27 referral document had been altered. Rather than have a recording of his IDAC meeting played, he told the commission he intended to lay criminal complaints against State Advocate Drushantha Ramsamy and to complain to the legal profession's regulator. Commissioner Sandile Khumalo SC put to him that he appeared to have gone along with a scheme to bolster the cases.
what_happened.tier_note: Tier 2 and Tier 3 reporting. Transcript not consulted.

why_it_matters:
Two different problems converged this week, and it is worth keeping them apart. The Matlala problem is structural: a person whose conduct sits at the centre of a commission's terms of reference also faces a pending criminal matter, and the privilege against self-incrimination is a real right, not a dodge. The commission cannot compel self-incriminating answers, so it is doing the only thing available — forcing the claim to be justified on affidavit, item by item, rather than asserted as a blanket. The direction with the 22 August deadline is the mechanism for that. Whether it produces answers on 24 and 25 August is the test.

The Adams problem is different, and goes to the reliability of the material that started a chain of investigations. His account has now shifted on the record across three sitting days: on how he obtained his information, on when he opened cases, on whom he contacted and how. If the section 27 affidavit that underpinned an IDAC investigation rests on a source who died in May 2025 and on documents the witness himself now says were altered, then the question in front of the commission is not only whether officials acted improperly but whether the trigger for their investigation was sound. That cuts in more than one direction, and the commission has not yet indicated which way it reads it.

The Day 161 documentary session matters for a third reason: it is the first material this week that does not depend on a witness's memory. Message traffic extracted from a device either says what it says or it does not. But it is also the evidence least tested — nobody was in the box to be questioned about it.
loose_ends: Matlala's supplementary affidavit, the replying affidavit and heads of argument were all due by 18:00 on 22 August 2026. Whether they were filed is unverified as at publication.

The commission adjourned on 20 August so Adams could listen to about two hours of IDAC recordings. It is not established from reporting whether that recording was in fact played on 21 August, or whether Adams's stated objection prevented it.
Adams says his section 27 referral document was altered. No source consulted records IDAC or Advocate Johnson responding to that specific allegation this week.

Adams said he would lay criminal complaints against Advocate Drushantha Ramsamy. Ramsamy has himself given evidence to the commission (Days 156 and 159). No response from him to this statement was located.
The commission did not establish whether any of the surveillance-equipment transactions discussed on Day 161 were completed. Absent that, the material shows negotiation, not acquisition.
Whether Adams's evidence concluded on 21 August is unclear; reporting says proceedings continue the following week.
Evidence-leader attributions across this week rest on one or two outlets each and in one case conflict. Advocate Mahlape Sello SC is named for Matlala by a single outlet.

new_faces.name: Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala
new_faces.note: First appearance in the witness box in this tracker's sample, on Day 160, under subpoena.
new_faces.status: Criminally charged in a separate matter

new_faces.name: Fadiel Adams
new_faces.note: Appeared on 11 August but his evidence was postponed; gave substantive evidence for the first time on Day 162.

new_faces.name: Steve Motsumi
new_faces.note: Named on Day 161 in message traffic about surveillance equipment. Has not appeared before the commission.

watch_next_week: Matlala's evidence resumes on Monday 24 and Tuesday 25 August 2026. The live question is how much of the self-incrimination claim survives the affidavit process.
Whether Adams concludes, and whether the IDAC recordings are played.
Whether IDAC, Advocate Andrea Johnson or Advocate Drushantha Ramsamy answer the altered-document allegation.
Whether the commission returns to the Msibi device material with a witness who can be questioned on it.
aside: Three sitting days of a witness correcting a witness, and the phrase that will outlive the week is a laptop that would not open its own email. The commission has heard testimony about R228-million contracts and IMSI-catchers, and the detail that stuck was IT support.
tier_summary: No Tier 1 source underpins this briefing. Everything here rests on Tier 2 and Tier 3 journalism plus broadcaster video titles. The commission's own transcripts, rulings and exhibit bundles were not accessible when this was compiled. Treat every claim as REPORTING unless it is marked RULING.
